records.name: Zeltīte
records.facts_used: Zeltīte is a Latvian name connected by Siliņš’s dictionary with zelts, gold. It brings together the precious metal’s name and a diminutive formation characteristic of Latvian. The dictionary also mentions a character in an Aspazija play, giving the name a literary as well as linguistic setting. The Latvian National Library holds Zeltīte: a drama in two acts, published by Gulbis in St Petersburg in 1904; its catalogue dates first publication to 1901. Separately, the name dictionary gives calendar inclusion in 1908. The play’s publication and the calendar entry are distinct milestones in the name’s history.
records.reason: Exact-form or explicitly scoped family evidence supports two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: 1904 is the held edition; 1901 is first publication in metadata and the encyclopaedia. Neither is a personal-name invention date.

records.name: Andijs
records.facts_used: The dictionary lists Andijs under Andis and connects Andis with Andrejs. This explicit chain leads to Greek andreios, manly or brave. The short form therefore retains a link with a wider name family, even when it is used independently in everyday life. The Andijs entry reports use in Saldus district in 1973, a concrete spelling record alongside the dictionary’s family connection. This place-and-year reference is neither the first use of Andis nor a date when Andijs entered the calendar.
records.reason: Exact-form or explicitly scoped family evidence supports two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Keep the exact spelling, country, dated record and publication scope distinct from a name-invention date.

records.name: Vilfrīds
records.facts_used: The dictionary connects Vilfrīds with Old High German willo, will, and fridu, peace or protection. These are the meanings of two historical name elements. It also notes an ī/ē variant, making the vowel spelling part of this family’s history. The Siliņš catalogue places Vilfrīds usage in the first quarter of the twentieth century and dates its calendar entry to 1966. Personal-name use and inclusion in a printed calendar are different records; 1966 should not be read as the name’s creation date.
records.reason: Exact-form or explicitly scoped family evidence supports two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Catalogue p.326, exact long-ī form. Do not infer unaccented feminine Vilfrida.

records.name: Vilibalds
records.facts_used: Vilibalds is a Latvian form in a Germanic name family. The dictionary connects its parts with Old High German willo, will, and bald, brave. These element glosses explain its structure without predicting the bearer’s character. The Vilibalds entry dates a calendar example as early as 1767, while its personal-use reference belongs to the first quarter of the twentieth century. The earlier printed calendar and later usage record are not contradictory: they describe different kinds of evidence.
records.reason: Exact-form or explicitly scoped family evidence supports two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: 1767 is a calendar record, not a bearer attestation.

records.name: Viliberts

These element meanings preserve the two-part structure of a Germanic naming tradition. The shared Vilberts/Viliberts dictionary material mentions use in 1894 and a calendar entry in 1966. This joint chronology is not independent proof of each spelling’s first occurrence. It shows how the source groups related forms within one historical entry.
records.reason: Exact-form or explicitly scoped family evidence supports two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Shared-entry dates retain their explicit scope; no independent Viliberts first-bearer date is asserted.

records.name: Zelta

The Zelta entry identifies a concrete use in Blome in 1931, providing a point in the Latvian history of this exact form. Zeltīte’s 1908 calendar date cannot automatically be transferred to Zelta, and the Blome record does not imply that the name was invented then.

records.name: Zlata
records.facts_used: The dictionary connects Zlata with Bulgarian and Serbo-Croatian zlato, gold. This Slavic name family thus has gold at its linguistic core. Latvian Zeltīte has a similar meaning, but a shared image does not by itself make the two names the same borrowing. The Latvian Language Agency’s rendering record pairs Russian Злата with Zlata, citing page 185 of Grabis and Porīte’s 1993 manual. This is a concrete spelling correspondence rather than a first-registration date or an account of every family’s route to the name.
records.reason: Exact-form or explicitly scoped family evidence supports two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Exact catalogue additionally reports 1973; no first-registration claim is made. The inspected LVA export cites the 1993 original, which was not independently reopened here.

records.name: Alberta
records.facts_used: Alberta is a feminine form of the Albert name family. Its Germanic elements are adal, noble, and berht, bright or famous. These roots explain the name’s historical structure without claiming noble ancestry for every bearer. The front page of Rokiškio Sirena dated 20 November 2015 lists Alberta among tomorrow’s name days, therefore referring to 21 November. This dated press example documents the exact form in Lithuanian calendar tradition rather than its first registration.
records.reason: Exact-form or explicitly scoped family evidence supports two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Keep the exact spelling, country, dated record and publication scope distinct from a name-invention date.

records.name: Honoratas
records.facts_used: Honoratas belongs to the Latin Honoratus family. Its Latin basis concerns honour and esteem, with Honoratus explained as honoured. This is the name’s linguistic inheritance rather than a statement about any particular bearer’s social position. The 1964 Tikiu Dievą calendar gives Honoratas with short forms Honas and Noras, reprinted in Salys’s 1983 volume. It places them on 21 December, whereas this calendar uses 21 November. The historical record documents the relationship without changing this calendar’s date.
records.reason: Exact-form or explicitly scoped family evidence supports two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: December/November discrepancy remains explicit; current membership unchanged.

records.name: Honorijus
records.facts_used: Honorijus is the Lithuanian form of Latin Honorius, in a family connected with honor, honour. Its historical meaning belongs to the sphere of honour and esteem. Honorijus and Honoratas share a Latin basis but are distinct full names. The Lithuanian encyclopaedia names the Roman ruler Flavijus Honorijus alongside Latin Flavius Honorius. He received the title Augustus in 393. This historical example demonstrates the Latin/Lithuanian spelling correspondence rather than a first registration of the name in Lithuania.
records.reason: Exact-form or explicitly scoped family evidence supports two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Use only checked Latin/Lithuanian pair and 393 Augustus title. Do not reuse the article’s problematic Ravenna chronology.
